Notes from Workshop I of the CEPS series on China’s industrial ecosystems: energy security and electrification, 2 September 2026. Presentations from CREA, Dialogue Earth and CAICT, and the discussion that followed, summarised by theme under the Chatham House rule.

Notes from Workshop II of the CEPS series on China’s industrial ecosystems: robotisation and AI governance, 12 October 2026. Four interventions, on the national level, Hangzhou, the Greater Bay Area and a European angle, and the discussion that followed, summarised by theme under the Chatham House rule.

Presentation 1 of 3Domestic energy policymaking (CREA)

Discussion

Slides shown · 5 · click to enlarge

Four drivers

Why China electrifies

1

Energy security

  • vast coal, but import-reliant on oil + gas
  • closure of Hormuz from March 2026 + the fossil price crisis
  • oil imports cut ~½, possible through electrification of transport plus stock management
2

Economic opportunity

  • cleantech + EVs named as future industries in the early 2000s
3

Air pollution

  • the original driver
  • millions of premature deaths in cities
4

Climate risk

  • Tibet/Nepal floods
  • physical risk framed as national security
From strategic priorities to industrial scale

top-down; the EU’s 2019 push was bottom-up

  1. 1
    National strategic direction + Five-Year Plans
  2. 2
    Sectoral planssteering industrial policy, finance, R&D, standards, infrastructure
  3. 3
    Provincial + local implementationcompeting for the projects and the best firms
  4. 4
    Competition in a large domestic marketcreating scale + integrated supply chains
  5. 5
    Falling costs, better productsmanufacturing advantage, export growth
Missing in the EU

the EU has no equivalent of the provincial-competition step

> rest of worldrenewables added, combined, for several years now
<50%coal in the power mix, H1 2026, first time: 49.7% of electricity, 52% of total energy
41%of generation from renewables; 22% of total energy, past the world average
~60%of new car sales are EVs: cars first, then mini + light trucks, buses
peakChina’s oil demand probably past it, at more than half of global demand growth
11.4%clean energy sectors’ share of GDP in 2025, from 7.3% in 2022
>30% · >90%of GDP growth and of investment growth
2inflection points passed: clean generation growth > demand growth; storage growth > peak demand growth

solar additions slowed sharply vs last year’s boom; wind better, nuclear picking up · framed as “new quality productive forces”, away from heavy industry and real estate · ministers have picked up CREA’s figures

Coal is the last big challenge, and still growing
2020/21 shortagesflexibility, price pass-through and weak hydro, not capacity
Response: capacity anyway~2 permits/week in 2022–23; last year the largest addition of coal capacity to the grid in a decade
Contractual obligationsPPAs of ~18 years; grid + transmission booked in advance; plants paid twice over, to stand by and to generate
Curtailmentend-of-year contract fulfilment drives curtailment of solar and wind
CO₂ +2%China’s CO₂ up ~2% in early 2026 on “wasted” wind + solar (CREA)
Utilisation

falling towards, probably below, 40% of the fleet on average, so retirement of part of the fleet becomes hard to avoid

New demand outlet

coal-to-chemicals pushed; sector emissions +~12% last year

15th Five-Year Plan signals

Strong on

  • clean supply
  • integration rather than deployment: modest deployment targets
  • storage, grids, power market reform, incentives for clean power in industry
  • direct supply to industrial sites and net-zero industrial parks

Weak on

  • emissions + fossil constraints
  • the 2021 pledge to gradually cut coal consumption has not been restated
Meaning for the EU?
1

look beyond the subsidies: competitiveness is structural and long-term

2

demand creation and infrastructure carry equal weight to manufacturing support

3

but do not import distortions: local incentives, coal lock-in, overcapacity

Power plants, average running hours

About 39% of the ceiling, all plant types, on NEA figures for 2025. Coal plants alone ran about 4,000 hours a year on CREA and GEM figures for the first half of 2026.

Discussion: domestic energy policymaking

ThemeWhat was said
Read the EU regionally, not in aggregate
  • battery-electric ~40% of new registrations in France; DE numbers worth a look
  • Bulgaria has the fastest uptake of storage with renewables
    • lignite collapse created a void entrepreneurs filled
Where the bottleneck sits
  • the system, or industrial uptake? Both
  • in the power system: the contract issue + advance grid booking
  • in industry: steel only ~10% electrified, 90% coal
    • chemicals worse, since coal chemicals are deliberately expanding
Central versus local
  • the EU analogue: energy union versus national security
  • national guidance deliberately leaves provinces room to interpret, and provinces differ enormously
    • Hainan against Xinjiang
Imports are not consumption
  • imports are usually a good proxy for consumption, not in 2026
    • can the decline in consumption be separated from the decline in imports?
  • the supply side is understood, the demand side is not
    • the electrostate argument: China is genuinely forcing demand into electricity
  • but of the oil import cut, ~70% was reserve management plus coal
    • only about a fifth to a quarter was additional renewable use
  • two constraints keep installed renewables out of consumption
    • (i) the grid cannot take it
    • (ii) coal’s price support keeps coal running
What the demand data show
  • imports fell ~50% but demand only ~3% in H1 and ~9% in Q2; stockpiles bridge it
    • oil is transport and petrochemicals, so it plays a small role in heating or power
  • the behavioural shift was fast
    • car sharing, EV use, hybrids actually charged
  • coal generation rose slightly in H1
  • CREA published the fuller breakdown on 3 September

Presentation 2 of 3Overseas energy investments (Dialogue Earth)

Discussion
Evolution in what the investment looks like
  1. before 2013the “going out” policya longer history of energy engagement abroad
  2. 2013BRI establishedenergy becomes the biggest sector for China’s investment in BRI countries
  3. early BRI yearscoal powernew markets for SOEs, while domestic coal construction was constrained at home
  4. 2021Xi’s UNGA pledgeend coal support overseas, increase green; effectively no new overseas coal plants since, with exceptions
  5. last year + H1not a total shiftrenewables well over half; most of the remainder oil + gas extraction
Exports
EVsbatteriessolarwindgrid technologies

rapid, steady growth; batteries and EVs stand out since the start of last year. Leading markets: Europe and Asia, with the same trend across the Global South.

Two ways out
State-steered
MOFCOM + NDRCapprove projects above a value threshold
State-owned firmsfound new markets through the BRI
Coal, then renewablesrenewables well over half last year and in H1
Market-pulled
Capacitypushes firms into any available export market
Individual entrepreneursalmost no Chinese state involvement
~75%of solar panels exported to Africa last year went to off-grid rooftops

The outward push is far less coordinated than the domestic model.

Institutional ecosystem
Top level
15FYP frames the BRI as “high-quality development”with internationalisation of Chinese renewable technology + standard-setting
Formal power
MOFCOM + NDRCapproval power above a value threshold
Informal steering
MEEholds no formal power, yet is the main force steering investment towards green tech. Its leverage runs through research institutes and organisations outside China
Semi-autonomous
Green Belt and Road Coalition · GEIDCOnon-binding research with real influence · State Grid-established non-profit pushing an integrated global grid, active in UN and climate forums

→ messy overall: many actors, guidelines without teeth, weak coordination

Market realities

capacity pushes firms to any available export market: the EU, Asia, and new and emerging markets including African countries

Least coordinated channel~75%of solar panels exported to Africa last year were purely off-grid rooftops

almost no Chinese state involvement: the actors are individual entrepreneurs; similarly batteries; decisive for energy access and SDG7

Host countries mediate

the Beijing picture is filtered through host policy (stakeholders and political economy). Pakistan’s finance ministry wrote its own pipeline; Indonesia and South Africa are proactive with different tactics

Anticipatory statecraft

foresight sits in domestic industrial policy; translation into foreign policy and trade is complex, and shaped from the receiving end

Discussion: overseas energy investments

ThemeWhat was said
Coal as a system asset
  • coal utilisation has fallen from a ceiling of ~8,100 full-load hours to ~3,150 (NEA)
    • coal is becoming a balancing asset rather than baseload
    • depreciation risk: run plants to end of life, not strand them
  • both main grids are building virtual power plants and demand response
    • principle: do not destroy before you are able to fill
  • lesson for Europe: take up the system-integration and engineering perspective
Cadre incentives
  • Central Committee + State Council measures on carbon peaking + neutrality
    • assessment and evaluation restructure the KPIs of local officials
      • weighted, system-engineering logic; first results this year
  • the provincial evaluation system is a promising systemic element of the 15FYP
    • interesting for the EU: how member states are held to climate targets
The overseas coal fleet
  • the same utilisation question is live for China-built plants in Pakistan and Vietnam
    • stranded assets and early retirement, driven mostly by non-government actors
  • some Pakistani plants are discussed as defaulting, undercut by Chinese-installed solar
  • where the 2021 pledge has not held, it is captive coal for industry
    • Indonesian nickel parks and some African steel plants
    • the exception appears in no document
Global grid, global posture
  • GEIDCO far more relevant now than it looked in 2016; joint documents with the JRC since 2018
  • China reluctant on fossil phase-out globally while domestically in the process
Capacity versus generation
  • solar is officially the largest source of installed capacity in China
    • but load factors differ by roughly 10–15×
  • coal still generates around eight times as much as the renewables compared
  • the real milestone is coal below 50% of generation, not the capacity crossover

CAICT is a think tank to the government under MIIT. Three parts:

1

Electrification for digital

2

Digitalisation for electrification

Coordination

Scale → IEA, Energy and AI
  • 415 TWh in 2024, ~1.5% of global electricity
  • ~945 TWh by 2030, roughly a doubling, driven by server numbers and power
  • ~12% growth a year since 2017: four times the growth of total global electricity
  • US, Europe and China account for ~85% of data-centre-related energy consumption
Electricity, not chips, is the binding constraint on AI.
Data centres in China’s electricity demand
about 1% todayabout 4% at four times today

Even four times today’s load stays small. Heavy and traditional industry matters far more.

Policy stack
15th Five-Year Plan
  • energy efficiency of computing facilities + 5G base stations
  • coordinated deployment of green electricity + computing power
  • new computing facilities to run primarily on non-fossil energy
“AI+ Energy” Implementation Opinions
  • preliminary AI → energy integration system by 2027; leading level by 2030
  • 8 application scenarios: grid, clean energy, hydro, thermal, nuclear, coal, O&G, plus emerging energy business models
Action Plan on the mutual empowerment of AI + energy
  • dual approach: 1. energy supports AI · 2. AI empowers the energy transition
Coordination as a national strategic requirement
  1. 2023Concept declareddeepening East Data West Computing, plus the national integrated computing power network
  2. 2024Goals setgreen + low-carbon data centre action plan + new electricity system plan 2024–27
  3. 2026National strategyGovernment Work Report + 15FYP Outline
Mechanism + instruments
West

renewables-rich, grid-short provinces take computing load

load →← green power
East

where computing demand sits

shift computing load to where the energy is, across space and across time · coordination starts at the data centre design stage · being written into standards, incl. at ITU, with Japan and the US in the discussions

1 · mandatoryPUE below 1.25for new large data centres; 1.5 is the target for the national average
2 · incentiveNational green data centres listpublished annually, with scoring
clean-power share, national computing hubs
~80% mandatoryother data centres face company, provincial and central requirements · 100% renewables would approach neutrality but is not realistic on cost
Challenges, as grouped by the presenter

Discussion: digital infrastructure

ThemeWhat was said
Europe’s digital–energy roadmap
  • the EU tech sovereignty package has a digitalisation and energy roadmap
    • same direction, much less advanced; the two entangled stacks not yet grasped
  • beyond interoperability → interconnectivity between data centres
    • the EU places factories and gigafactories without connecting them
Efficiency by constraint
  • electrification and sustainability of AI infrastructure matter more in China than the US
  • DeepSeek: constrained GPUs produced a more energy-efficient path
    • open question: did well-timed policy give that innovation its directionality?
  • China’s productivity growth comes largely from energy, elsewhere from tech
  • Berkeley reflects on the same entanglement, but it is not translating into government priorities
Where the money goes
  • AI venture capital over 10–15 yrs: ~11% military, ~10% aviation, 0.4% energy
    • is the Chinese split different?
  • AI investment in China up more than 20% last year against 2024; no separate energy figure
East Data West Computing in practice
  • storage and processing move to the energy-rich west, but data centres need proximity to users
    • hence Shanghai ambitions, incl. undersea
  • green electricity certificates changed: 80% must now be sourced regionally
  • scale: data centres are ~1% of China’s electricity demand, so even 4× leaves ~4%
    • heavy and traditional industry matters far more
  • the new concept is computing power and electric power coordination, broader than EDWC
  • what digitalisation gives industry: carbon and energy reduction; the payback is cost
The US picture
  • the clean-energy push is at state, not federal level
    • California now above half clean electricity
  • the frontier is clean energy plus digitalisation of the network

Summary

Main points

  • Coal’s long contracts mean solar and wind get curtailed→
  • Local officials are now assessed on carbon peaking and neutrality, with first results this year→
  • Provinces compete for the projects and the best firms; the EU has no equivalent step→
  • China now plans electricity and computing together→
  • Overseas energy investment has many actors, guidelines without teeth and weak coordination→
  • Of the oil import cut, ~70% was reserve management and coal; only a fifth to a quarter came from more renewables→
01

The difference is in the share

  • China put the sustainability of the grid for AI installations up front in strategy
  • the resulting coordination between the two stacks is seen neither in the EU nor the US
    • where the discussion is about adding SMRs to data centres to sustain the load
  • China is getting better and better at our own game, and we can learn from that
02

Lessons to learn for the EU

  • demand before, or alongside, supply: targets, infrastructure and clean shares
    • EU funds the factories and leaves the demand signal vague
  • subnational implementation needs restructured incentives, not just targets
    • carbon peaking/neutrality measures are the instrument to watch
  • treat digital and energy as one system
    • load shifting as a grid resource, and interconnection between data centres
  • plan legacy-asset retirement and replacement flexibility together
03

Consequences for Europe

  • China cleantech competitiveness cannot be argued away as subsidy: the push is structural
    • off-grid Africa and the recipient pipelines (PK, ID, ZA) are where EU offers compete
  • coal’s contract + curtailment = case that capacity is not delivered generation

Intervention 1 of 4China’s embodied-AI + robotics ecosystem, national level

Two markets, not one
~295,000industrial robots installed in 2024 (IFR)
54%of global installations, a base of customers, suppliers + engineering experience
144humanoid companies in 2025, with 336 products (source-reported)
~17,000humanoid shipments in 2025 (source-reported)
>50financing rounds in Q1 2026
~RMB 20bnraised in those rounds: complete robots, models, dexterous hands, computing, data

embodied AI = systems that perceive, reason + act through a physical body · other market boundaries + maturity → robot counts are context, not a measure of embodied AI · quadrupeds, AVs + drones use other definitions, not to be added up

Technical routes
  1. firstrules
  2. thenlearning
  3. since 2022foundation models
  4. nowfour routes in parallel(i) language models, (ii) vision-language, (iii) vision-language-action, (iv) world models → no settled architecture

the ecosystem needs robotics engineering + models, data + computing

Where the companies sit

Company counts, not revenue. The top three regions hold 62.8% of the companies, the top five 82.1%.

Division of labour

spans applications, products, technology services, infrastructure (models, data, integration) + sensing, actuation, computing, platforms

Inputs
specialist supplierssensing, computing, dexterous hands
Intelligence
models, simulation, data
Platforms
complete platforms + integrationUnitree, AgiBot, UBTech
Users
industry customers + system integratorsclose the chain

→ the interfaces between them are why standards matter

Deployment model as a distinctive advantage

coordination between technical supply + real operating demand

  1. 1
    Public programmesshared facilities + application opportunities
  2. 2
    Platform firms + specialistssupply the inputs
  3. 3
    Lead customers + integratorsdefine tasks, operating conditions + acceptance criteria
  4. 4
    Commercial demand decidesrepeated deployment + learning at manageable integration cost
Caveat

subsidised demonstrations alone do not create sustainable demand

Readiness = task complexity × how understandable the environment is

First

  • research
  • education
  • inspection
  • selected logistics

Second

  • home assistance
  • extreme environments

mobility in structured environments is easier than manipulation in changing surroundings

Not only humanoids
humanoidsquadrupedsarmsAVsdronesvesselsglassestransformable platformsswarm micro-robotswearables

do not equate embodied AI with humanoids

Barriers
  • reliability in unfamiliar conditions, long action sequences, data quality, integration cost, safety
  • evidence beyond demos
    • task success, human intervention, cost per completed task
Standards
MIIT + the AI standardisation committee (embodied-intelligence working group)
  • requirements, data quality, system performance
Two sector standards
  • benchmarking + assessment methodology, in force since June 2026
  • dataset quality, published, due Nov 2026
  • further work: training facilities, interfaces, platforms, capability levels, safety
CAICT benchmark
  • >30,000 test tasks, >300 task types, atomic skills to long sequences

→ a benchmark is not a certification

Standards vs dependency

Lock-in risks

  • proprietary connectors
  • vendor-specific control
  • non-portable task data
  • exclusive testing

Questions to ask

  • interfaces documented?
  • data exportable with metadata?
  • tasks reproducible?
  • multi-vendor conformance tests?

standards cut integration cost; the effect depends on implementation

Distribution: vocational skills policy
  • subsidised training tied to industry demand + digital/AI skills
    • >30m participants targeted 2025–27, economy-wide
    • not a robotics target, not a measure of transitions → link adoption programmes to employment outcomes
Four implications for European competitiveness
1

aggregate industrial demand around concrete use cases + common acceptance tests

2

give smaller firms access to test facilities + integration support

3

portable data + interfaces, incl. through international standards

4

connect adoption with training + employment outcomes

proposals, not a description of Europe · China’s lesson: supplier-user-feedback-standards connections matter alongside breakthroughs

Intervention 3 of 4The Greater Bay Area

Two structural features
1

world-class manufacturing base: 9 Guangdong cities + Hong Kong + Macau; >40% of China’s industrial robots made in Guangdong → top producer + top adopter

2

largest + densest migrant population

Economic dimension
  • deployment unusually fast (Midea, GAC, Gree fully automated) but uneven: large firms afford it, most SMEs cannot
    • the Greater Bay Area depends on SMEs more than other provinces → the gap widens without support
Three steps for SMEs
  1. 1
    Clusters“upstairs is upstream, downstairs is downstream” → draw a part in the morning, prototype in the afternoon, iterate next day · component costs down by orders of magnitude; each city a specialty (Shenzhen chips, Dongguan parts), all within ~2 hours · XbotPark (Dongguan, professor-founded): shared factory from concept to mass production, 80% of its firms survive
  2. 2
    Shared infrastructureembodied-intelligence training facility under construction in Guangzhou
  3. 3
    SOEs help SMEsdistrict digital-transformation centres diagnose, subsidise, supply local computing, integrate on site, stretch payment to 3–5 months; almost every city/district has one
Race to be first: quality sometimes loses

China

  • moves fast + regulates later
  • humanoid half-marathon falls, trust crises

Europe

  • regulates first

neither extreme comfortable → middle ground through cooperation

Equity
  • platform rents widen the gap
    • employment-impact assessment
    • redistribute part of platform returns
    • a capital tax for social insurance
Social dimension: impact moved from forecast to reality
  • driving is the fallback job
    • most entered after losing manufacturing jobs; active ones earn <RMB 200/day
  • broad decline across manufacturing + services
Labour rights under pressure
falling piece ratesunpaid waiting timeweak social insurancelittle bargaining room
Responses so far
  • China announced an action plan on employment amid AI last week, no details yet
  • occupational insurance, lifelong study, firms (Lalamove, Meituan) with 24h services, skills competitions, rider homes
  • the fundamental one: support real firms, enterprises create jobs; government holds the bottom line
Proposals
  • AI employment monitoring (Singapore’s job dictionaries)
    • tell workers which jobs exist, subsidies, cheaper basic services for migrants
    • fear of losing income is the barrier to retraining
  • the human side: workers controlled by AI, work without judgement
    • “social atomisation” as fewer belong to a stable enterprise
    • public governance cannot rely on private platforms

Intervention 4 of 4The European angle

Coordination: very little is left purely to the market
  • hardware, robotics, manufacturing ecosystems, physical + data infrastructure = one system, coordinated centrally + locally
    • hybrid forms between governance actors, S&T institutes + private firms → much for Europe to learn
Supporting resources
Energy
the “world’s first electrostate”the answer to Middle East instability, not wars of choice; coal below half the mix
Compute
East Data West Computing + the national unified computing-power networkcompute as a utility “out of the wall”
Money: two political economies

Europe

  • prosperity from profit: the numbers must go up
  • what does not lift them is punished by bond markets + investors

China

  • prosperity from availability + affordability
  • investment led by competitive local governments
  • → involution: fierce competition, high quality, low prices, no profit (the Econ 101 perfect market)
Two systems that kept each other alive
  • Europe needs deflationary goods while asset prices rise, China needs export markets
    • now China is no longer the cheap source + threatens the most profitable sectors (cars)
  • robots automate far more work: productivity + affordability, but what do displaced people do
    • maybe the first time there are no new things to do
    • what is an economy for, what distribution is appropriate
  • a model that makes parts of the economy uninvestable (margins → 0) reaches the whole European financial structure in three or four steps
The problems are political, not intellectual: “do more of what China does” will not fix them.

Discussion

ThemeWhat was said
Where the money comes from: guidance funds and IPO signals
  • the Hangzhou fund (~USD 280m?) → where does the money come from, guidance funds, how big a role, do they come first + signal the IPO
    • regional differences
Pension money as Europe’s missing venture capital
  • Silicon Valley came from a 1970s change in US pension law
  • EU pension + insurance money in VC ≈ 1/100 of 1% of holdings → balance of China’s sources?
Patient city capital: Hangzhou’s fund and Hefei’s three bets
  • the fund: set up by the city via its state-owned asset company, not big
    • early-stage, long-term, not profit-sensitive
    • aim = attract entrepreneurs
  • Hefei: Changxin Memory (CXMT), no. 4 in DRAM after Micron, Samsung, SK hynix; ten years of city money while VCs stayed away, now going public
    • three bets in ~10 years: BOE (displays), NIO (EV industry), CXMT
  • a patient city builds industries from scratch
Foresight or patient capital?
  • DRAM: foresight that memory becomes critical (GPU/CPU-memory coupling, in-memory processing) or patient capital spotting a market gap?
    • technically possible
    • the key is who bears ten years of losses + management changes
    • entrepreneur + city + capital together, bankruptcy risk included
Are frontier AI models moving into robots?
  • not yet: an LLM predicts the next token, a robot needs concrete, explainable, trustworthy physical action
    • LLMs help with cognition, not acts
  • the data differs: human text vs practical data from teleoperated robots (hands, fingers, arms) → VLA models
    • nobody knows the right way
    • scaling-law view: one end-to-end model, not chained models for cognition, decision, execution
  • AI works in closed worlds (rules settled, feedback automatic)
    • autonomous driving is the closest to closed; open world not yet
China legislates too: standards first, then law
  • only partly true that Europe legislates + China innovates: clear industrial mandate + comprehensive legislation on AI + robotics
    • standards first: humanoid/embodied-intelligence standards Feb 2026 + the 15th FYP mandate, five years in the making; MIIT key standards by 2028
    • pilots, then higher-level law; the 2026 ecological-environmental code is the arrival point; parallel processes, adjust on results
  • China sees the EU as irrelevant (22% presence in its supply chains) but the EU holds strategic capabilities: industrial internet, virtual twins
    • cooperation potential Italy/Germany-China on manipulation + standards, under regulation with red lines
  • data centres: eco-design central, fewer than the US (a financial decision); ~77,000–100,000 STEM PhDs a year vs ~44,000 in the US
Not how much Europe borrows, but what for
  • not debt aversion: the Netherlands has 130% of GDP in mortgages → the question is what to borrow for; welfare + health over half the budget
  • Silicon Valley conditions absent: large but not single market, fragmented where network effects + scale matter
  • capital discipline: CSIS puts China’s EV subsidies at ~USD 230bn over 2009–23
    • < half of Dutch government spending in one year ≈ the three German carmakers’ dividends + buybacks over a decade → the money goes to wealthy people + legacy industries

Open questions and next seminars
  • many questions left; follow-ups
    • provincial experimentation + piloting
    • location of investment (factories, gigafactories) + fibre for west-east workloads
    • the Economist on China’s six networks
    • data sharing (data spaces, industrial data)
    • regional technological specialisation
  • a body of knowledge on the Chinese experience not yet accumulated in Brussels
    • next seminars to follow
